paras: The lynching of George Parrott, known as "Big Nose George," took place in Rawlins, Wyoming Territory, on the night of March 22, 1881, when a party of men took the condemned prisoner from the county jail and hanged him from a telegraph pole. Parrott had been sentenced to death for the killing of two deputy sheriffs and had tried to break jail earlier that evening. The story ran in papers from California to Rhode Island, which dwelt on the escape attempt, the failed first hanging and his last words.

Newspapers described Parrott as one of the "Elk Mountain murderers" and an "infamous road agent." According to the Morris Tribune, his gang had tried to wreck and rob a Union Pacific train near Medicine Bow, and deputy sheriffs Tip Vincent and Widdowfield, who followed them, were killed. The Omaha Bee added that his confederate "Dutch Charley" had already been taken from a train and lynched, and that Parrott was captured in Montana, narrowly escaping lynching there, before being tried in Carbon County.

He was reported to have confessed and pleaded guilty, and he was sentenced to hang, most papers said on April 2. Weeks before, the Cheyenne Leader's Rawlins notes said he was "not as sick as reported."

On the evening of March 22 Parrott got free of his shackles and struck jailer Robert Rankin on the head with them as Rankin entered the corridor to lock the cells. The Omaha Bee said he had filed them off with a file obtained from a fellow prisoner. Rankin's wife locked the door and stopped the escape, and citizens who answered the alarm released the jailer and secured the prisoner. The Cheyenne wire noted that sympathy for Parrott gave way to "threats of lynching."

At about 10:55 that night, according to the Leader's Rawlins special, a party of masked men took him from the jail to a telegraph pole opposite the railroad machine shops, near the depot. They first stood him on a barrel and kicked it away, but he was only choked, so they made him climb a ladder with the rope around his neck. His last words were reported as "I will jump off, boys, and break my neck." The drop did not break his neck; he freed his hands, climbed several feet up the pole and begged to be shot, then let go and died.

The coroner cut down the body, and the AP dispatch said an inquest would be held. No report of the inquest's finding or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage. The Omaha Bee's Rawlins correspondent wrote that the lynching was the town's chief topic and that praise was given to the citizens who rid the community of the "ruffian."

Most papers carried the Cheyenne wire, often in two parts: the foiled escape and then the Leader's special on the hanging. Headlines featured the mob and the pole, as in the Wheeling Register's "Strung Up to a Telegraph Post" and the Evening Star's "Hanged by a Mob." The West Virginia Argus subheaded its version "A Wyoming Criminal Who Expressed a Willingness to Co-operate With His Self-Appointed Executioners."

Later weeklies printed fuller narratives. The Juniata Sentinel told of a masked party riding into town and closed with the line that "the Elk Mountain murder was avenged," while the Morris Tribune called the lynching "quietly conducted." Brief notices in the Batesville Guard and American Citizen dated the event to the night of the 23d, and the Narragansett Herald named the victim "George F. Warden." The Louisiana Capitolian treated it as a "dramatic" Far-Western incident in which "Judge Lynch intervened, shortened his sentence by a few days." None of the papers mentioned race.

Accounts differ on who did it: the Leader and the wire said masked men, the AP dispatch "a mob," and the Morris Tribune and Jamestown Alert the citizens of Rawlins. The Juniata Sentinel said Sheriff Rankin and his deputies were overpowered, whereas the AP dispatch said no attempt was made to prevent the lynching. Reported times range from 10:50 to midnight, and the scheduled execution date appears as April 2, 24 or 26.

reader.title: Lynching of George Parrott (Big Nose George)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A party described as masked men, a mob or the citizens of Rawlins took a condemned prisoner from the Rawlins jail and hanged him from a telegraph pole (A3, A5, A13, A19).

Parrott died after being hanged by a group variously called 'a party of masked men', 'a mob' and 'citizens of Rawlins' who took him from the jail without legal authority (A3, A13, A19); the papers tie the act to his murder conviction and to fear he would escape the gallows (A17, A25).

The local Leader special (A3), the separate Omaha Bee special and AP dispatch (A13) and the later 'particulars' story (A19) agree that he was taken from the jail and hanged from a telegraph pole the night of March 22.

accounts.gist: After a failed jail break, a party of masked men took him from the jail at 10:55 p.m. and hanged him from a telegraph pole by a ladder; his last words were 'I will jump off, boys, and break my neck.'

accounts.label: AP dispatch and Omaha Bee special
accounts.gist: When news of the attack on the jailer spread, a mob took him from the jail with no attempt made to prevent it; the barrel failed, he climbed the pole after his hands came loose, and the coroner took the body.

accounts.label: Juniata Sentinel narrative
accounts.gist: A masked party rode into town about 10:30, demanded the keys, overpowered the sheriff and deputies, and rode away after hanging him at the depot.

accounts.label: 'Particulars' story
accounts.gist: Citizens of Rawlins assembled, took him from jail, and hanged him at a pole near the depot in a lynching 'quietly conducted'.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Cheyenne wire under headlines such as 'BIG NOSE GEORGE LYNCHED' and 'Strung Up to a Telegraph Post', calling him an 'infamous road agent'.
The Omaha Bee's Rawlins special reported praise for the citizens who rid the community of the 'red handed ruffian'; the Juniata Sentinel ended 'the Elk Mountain murder was avenged'.
The Louisiana Capitolian treated it as a 'dramatic' Far-Western incident in which 'Judge Lynch intervened', calling the victim 'gamely courteous'.

info: Night of March 22, 1881 (Tuesday); a few briefs say 'the night of the 23d'
Rawlins, Wyoming Territory: taken from the jail to a telegraph pole opposite the railroad machine shops, near the depot
George Parrott (also Parrot, Parratt), alias 'Big Nose George' or 'Big-Nosed George'; one paper calls him 'George F. Warden'. No paper states his race.

Under sentence of death for murder: described as one of the 'Elk Mountain murderers' who killed deputy sheriffs Tip Vincent and Widdowfield after a failed attempt to wreck a Union Pacific train; he had confessed and pleaded guilty. That evening he also attacked the jailer in an escape attempt.
'A party of masked men' (Leader special and wire); 'a mob' (AP, Star, Chicago Tribune); 'citizens of Rawlins' (Morris Tribune, Jamestown Alert). None named.
